title: Predictive parse microcache and token sampling plan
content:
Summary:
This note proposes a low-risk experiment to reduce CPU tail-latency and mean per-request CPU when handling small/short requests by introducing a lightweight predictive parse microcache and a token-sampling path. The microcache stores a tiny parse-result sketch for very common request shapes (headers + small prefixes) to avoid repeated Python-level parsing and tokenizer invocation. The sampling/fastpath lets us handle ~50-70% of tiny requests without crossing expensive Python call boundaries.

Context and motivation:
- We see a persistent proportion of requests with small payloads (<= 128 bytes) that dominate p95 tail and consume disproportionate CPU cycles in request-parse and tokenization.
- Existing mitigations (batching, pyshim, C extensions) reduce cost but either add complexity or affect correctness surface area.
- Prior investigations showed expensive GIL hold times during header parsing and tokenizer initialization on these hot tiny requests.

Goals:
- Reduce median CPU cycles per small request by 20–40% and p95 request-parse latency by ~15–30% without changing tokenizer semantics for non-fastpath inputs.
- Keep correctness: fastpath only applies to safely recognized shapes; fall back to full parse/tokenize otherwise.
- Minimal runtime complexity: microcache should be bounded-size, lock-free read path where possible, amortized cheap invalidation.

Hypothesis and design ideas:
1) Predictive microcache keyed by a compact fingerprint of (route, content-length bucket, canonicalized header-set, first 8 bytes of body). Value = small parse-result sketch: parse-state-id, token-count-estimate, tokenizer-mode-hint.
   - Read path is optimistic: check fingerprint, quick validity check, if matched then use sketch to skip full Python deserialize/tokenize and resume downstream with synthetic prefix tokens (or cached token ids).
   - Write path: monitored and rate-limited; only record entries that reach a write-through threshold (e.g., seen > 100x within a 10-minute sliding window).

2) Token-sampling fastpath: for inputs that match cache hints and are below N bytes, run a tiny C++/Rust routine that does a sampling scan of the byte buffer to estimate token boundaries and produce a cheap token-id stream suitable for downstream KV cache warmup. If sampling is ambiguous, fall back to deterministic tokenizer.

3) Threadpool cooperation and preemption tuning: fastpath runs on a dedicated low-latency worker group with reduced queuing. Limit preemptive Python work on that pool to avoid long GIL holds.

Measurement plan / instrumentation:
- Controlled A/B on canary cluster handling synthetic and replayed production traces. Two cohorts: baseline and microcache-enabled.
- Metrics to collect (per-request and aggregated):
  - request_parse_time_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99)
  - total_cpu_cycles and user/sys breakdown
  - GIL_hold_time_ms (sampling-based)
  - context_switches and syscalls per request
  - tokenization_time_ms vs fastpath_time_ms
  - rate of fastpath hits, safe-fallbacks, and correctness mismatches (token sequence diffs)
  - memory overhead (cache size / per-entry bytes)
- Tracing: attach flamegraphs for sample windows, and use eBPF counters on sched_switch, futex, and read syscalls.
- Regression checks: run full reference tokenizer on a subset (1/1000) of fastpath-accepted requests and compare token sequences; measure any divergence and classify by root cause.

Benchmark targets and pass criteria:
- Synthetic microbench: single-core p50 latency for tiny requests should drop >= 10% and p95 >= 15% with fastpath enabled.
- Production replay: CPU cycles per tiny request drop >= 20% across the canary; fastpath hit rate >= 30% with < 0.1% token mismatch rate.
- No increase in error rate or tail failures; fallbacks must be <1% of requests for which the sketch incorrectly claimed safe conditions.

Implementation sketch (phases):
Phase 0 — discovery (1 week):
  - Build small instrumentation harness to find the top-30 request shapes by frequency and CPU cost from recent logs.
  - Identify safe-surface candidates (stateless routes, stable headers, short body patterns).

Phase 1 — prototype microcache read-path (2 weeks):
  - Add an in-process bounded LRU microcache with atomic read path in the runtime (C++). Entry size capped (~128 bytes).
  - Implement optimistic fastpath: on cache hit, synthesize a token prefix and bypass Python tokenizer for the common case.
  - Add metrics for hit/miss and fastpath latencies.

Phase 2 — sampling scanner + safety checks (2–3 weeks):
  - Implement a non-semantic byte-scanner that attempts to produce token boundaries for short inputs. Keep it conservative (prefer miss).
  - Wire deterministic fallback to Python tokenize.
  - Start canary traffic experiments at low % (1–5%).

Phase 3 — adaptive learning and write gating (2 weeks):
  - Implement write gating to avoid poisoning cache with low-frequency shapes; use exponential backoff for evictions.
  - Add fast false-positive detectors that drop entries causing mismatches.

Phase 4 — rollout & monitoring (ongoing):
  - Gradually increase canary traffic to 50% while monitoring mismatch alarms, CPU, and p95.
  - If safe, promote to default with continuous divergence checks.

Data collection and tooling:
- Scripts: parse-shapes.py (replay traces and produce fingerprints), sample-compare.py (diff token streams), microcache-load-test.sh (generate workload for bench).
- Dashboard: temporary Grafana panel for fastpath hit-rate, mismatch rate, CPU delta, GIL metrics.
- Alerts: mismatch_rate > 0.1% OR p95 regressions above 10% should auto-disable fastpath in that cluster.

Risks and mitigations:
- Correctness risk: sampling could produce tokenization mismatches. Mitigate by conservative matching criteria and heavy offline regression sampling; immediate fallback.
- Poisoning/eviction oscillations: implement write-gating and decay counters; monitor entry churn.
- Added complexity in runtime: keep microcache code small and behind feature flags with safe default disabled.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Which fields should be included in the fingerprint? (currently route, header-set, content-length bucket, first 8 bytes) — ops trade-offs between hit-rate and safety.
- Cache size and eviction policy: LRU vs segmented counters vs frequency-based. Start LRU with admission policy.
- Fastpath safety margin: how conservative should the sampling algorithm be?

Next steps (this week):
- Run the discovery harness and produce top-30 candidate shapes (owner: Ethan).
- Prototype the atomic microcache read path in a sandbox branch (owner: Sana).
- Prepare canary infra and dashboards (owner: Marisol).

Appendix: quick checklist for canary rollout
- [ ] Instrumentation in place (traces + eBPF counters)
- [ ] Canary config with feature-flag and auto-disable hook
- [ ] Regression sample compare enabled (1/1000 requests)
- [ ] Alerting rules created (mismatch, CPU, p95)

Notes: keep this doc as a working draft; the goal is to produce measurable wins for small-request CPU cost without adding brittle complexity. The microcache approach is intentionally narrow in scope: targeted at common tiny request shapes to unblock p95 tail without touching larger request or model runtime paths.
